notes.meaning: The gold of the temple has lost its shine, and sacred gems lie dumped on every street corner. When the city fell, holy treasures were pulled down and trampled in the dirt. This shows how quickly great beauty and honour can be ruined by sin.

The precious people of Jerusalem were once valued like fine gold, but now they are treated like cheap clay pots. In ancient times, clay jars were easily broken and tossed away without a thought. The enemy treated God's treasured people as if they had no worth at all.

Even wild jackals feed and care for their puppies, but the starving mothers of Jerusalem have become distant like ostriches. Ostriches were known for laying their eggs in the sand and leaving them unattended. The brutal famine made parents unable to care for their own children.

Starving babies have no milk, so their tongues stick to the roofs of their mouths from thirst. Young children beg their parents for bread, but no one has anything to give them. The famine in the city left even the most helpless without food or drink.

People who grew up eating delicious meals now wander starving through the streets. Those who wore royal purple and scarlet clothing must search for warmth and food in piles of garbage. The siege stripped away all wealth and brought everyone down into the dust.

Jerusalem's suffering was more painful than the sudden destruction of ancient Sodom. Sodom was wiped out in a single moment by God's hand without people laying a siege against her. Jerusalem had to endure many months of starving and watching loved ones die.

Jerusalem's nobles and dedicated leaders were once healthy and glowing with vigor. Their skin looked pure and bright, like clean snow and sparkling gems. They showed the beauty and blessing of God's favour on their lives.

Now these same leaders have skins blacker than soot from starvation, and their bodies are as thin and dry as sticks. They are so changed by hunger that friends in the street do not even recognize them. Suffering and famine completely erased their former glory.

Those killed quickly in battle were more fortunate than those dying of starvation. A sword wound brought death in a short time, but hunger caused people to waste away in lingering pain. The destruction of the crops left them with no relief in sight.

Women who were once gentle and loving were driven by starving agony to boil their own babies for food. The desperate hunger of the siege overcame natural motherly love. This terrible act fulfilled the ancient warnings about the extreme horrors of war.

The Lord poured out all His anger and sent a consuming fire against Jerusalem. This judgment was so deep that it burned down the very stone foundations of the city. It showed that God's patience had ended and His sentence against sin was carried out.

Kings and nations across the world never believed that an invading army could enter Jerusalem. The city had powerful stone walls and a long history of divine protection. Its sudden fall proved to everyone that God Himself had allowed the Babylonians inside.

The city fell because its priests and false prophets had committed terrible sins and killed righteous people. These religious leaders used their positions to mislead the public instead of calling them away from evil. When leaders corrupt God's truth, ruin soon follows for the whole nation.

These corrupt priests and prophets wandered blindly through the streets in shock and confusion. Their robes were soaked with innocent blood, making them completely unclean under God's law. No one dared to touch them because of their terrible crimes.

Crowds shouted at these guilty leaders to get away, treating them like lepers who were spiritually defiled. When they tried to flee to other countries, foreign people refused to give them a home. The leaders who once acted proud were now rejected everywhere they went.

The Lord Himself scattered the people in His anger and stopped looking on them with favour. The invading army showed no respect to elderly people or honoured priests. God let their leaders be humbled because they had dishonoured Him.

The people strained their eyes from watchtowers looking for an ally like Egypt to rescue them, but no help came. Human treaties and foreign armies failed to deliver Jerusalem from the Babylonians. Trusting in worldly allies instead of the Lord always ends in deep disappointment.

The enemy tracked the citizens' every move from siege mounds, making it deadly to walk out in the streets. The defenders knew that their days were numbered and the end of their nation had arrived. There was no way to escape the net tightening around them.

The Babylonian cavalry chased fleeing Judeans faster than eagles diving through the air. They hunted them through the mountain paths and set ambushes in the plains. Nobody could outrun the swift judgment that had arrived.

King Zedekiah, the anointed ruler whom the people viewed as the very breath of their nation, was captured in the enemy's net. The people had hoped to survive together under his protection, even as a small kingdom among pagan nations. His capture wiped out their last hope of human security.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The traditional Latin version translates this phrase as 'Christ the Lord,' seeing the captured king as a type pointing forward to Jesus.

notes.meaning: The neighboring country of Edom cheered when Jerusalem fell, but the prophet warns that their joy will not last. Edom will also have to drink the cup of God's wrath and be left disgraced. Gloating over the misfortunes of others only invites the same judgment upon oneself.

The Lord announces that Jerusalem's time of exile and punishment is coming to a close. However, the nation of Edom will soon face punishment, and their sins will be laid bare. God's people have the hope of coming mercy, while their unrepentant enemies face sure ruin.

differ.view: Many Baptists understand Zion's completed punishment as pointing to Christ on the cross, who bore the full penalty of sin so that God asks for no further payment from believers.
